Model checking as model building: length of stay in the RHC/SUPPORT study

An in-class walkthrough for the Linear Regression II chapter

Support study

  • SUPPORT trial 1989-1994 tested an intervention to improve end-of-life decision making and reduce mechanically supported, painful, and prolonged process of dying.
  • Intervention: Physicians and their seriously ill admitted patients were randomized at the physician level to receiving daily estimates of 6 month survival for each patient and nursing support to work on a) eliciting preferences, b) helping family understand predicted outcomes, c) facilitate advanced plannng and d) communication.
  • Design: 2-year prospective observational study (phase I - 4301 patients) then a 2-year clinical trial (phase II) that randomized clinical services or specialty groups with their patients (2652-intervention, 2152 control). (A cluster was defined as a distinct clinical service or subspecialty group at a hospital, e.g. all the attending physicians and residents assigned to the Cardiology Service, General Internal Medicine Team A, or the Pulmonary/Critical Care Service)

Support/RHC Study

  • Emebeded within Support Trial (Connors et al., 1996)
  • MotivationLevaluate the clinical effectiveness of Right Heart Catheterization (RHC)—also known as a Swan-Ganz catheter—in the initial 24 hours of adult care in the intensive care unit (ICU).
  • RHC was widely used but with little evidence supporting use
  • (enough) Clinicians strong belief in the benfit precluded RCT.
  • Design: Prospective cohort study. N=5734 patients from the parent SUPPORT study
  • Inclusion:
    • admitted to the ICU in the first 24 hours
    • fit one of 9 pre-specified diagnostic categories
    • complete covariate data recorded in the first 24 hours.

Load the data (load_data)

1. Model of predictors of length of stay (LOS)

  • Question
  • Hint
  • Answer

We want to describe how hospital length of stay varies across ICU patients.

  • One of the advantages of SUPPORT was the comprehensive severity of illness data summarized in the 2 and 6 month survival prediction.
  • Knaus (the APACHE developer) was an investigator and the acute physiology score on day 1 is part of the prediction model.

Fit a model on disease category, day-1 predicted survival, age, and sex (round1):

use rhc_class_tph.dta, clear
generate los = dschdte - sadmdte
drop if missing(los) | los <= 0
regress los i.cat1 c.surv2md1 c.age i.sex

The coefficient table looks reasonable and most predictors are “significant”

Are we done?

Try simulating an outcome from the fitted model and compare to the data.

A normal-error model spreads predictions symmetrically around the mean.

Fit the model, then simulate one dataset from it and count how many stays are negative: (replicate ans_x2d)

regress los i.cat1 c.surv2md1 c.age i.sex
set seed 20260912
qui predict double xb_naive
generate double los_sim = xb_naive + rnormal(0, e(rmse))
count if los_sim < 0
twoway (kdensity los, lcolor(navy) lwidth(thick)) ///
       (kdensity los_sim, lcolor(cranberry) lwidth(thick)), ///
       xline(0, lpattern(dash) lcolor(red)) ///
       legend(order(1 "Observed LOS" 2 "Simulated from model") ring(0) pos(2)) ///
       xtitle("Length of stay (days)") ///
       title("The model invents impossible negative stays")
qui graph export img/rhc_naive_sim.png, replace width(1400)

More than a thousand simulated patients have a negative length of stay. A stay cannot be negative, so the model is already telling us it is the wrong shape for this outcome.

2. What does the outcome look like overall and across predictors?

  • Question
  • Hint
  • Answer-1
  • Answer-2
  • Answer-3
  • Answer-4
  • take-home

Think about functional form and graph the data.

  1. What does LOS look like raw vs. logged?
  2. How does it differ across primary disease category?
  3. How does it differ by DNR status and by in-hospital death?
  4. How does it change across a severity range (day-1 predicted survival)?
  • histogram of los and of ln(los) — is either roughly symmetric?
  • graph hbox over cat1 — do the differences make sense?
  • kdensity by dnr1 and by diedhosp — does LOS mix distinct groups?
  • lowess of LOS on surv2md1, pooled and then split by diedhosp — is the pooled shape a single trend or a mixture?

Raw vs. log. The raw outcome is heavily right-skewed with a floor at zero; the log scale is roughly symmetric. (raw_vs_log)

histogram los, width(10) fcolor(midblue%40) lcolor(white) ///
    xtitle("Length of stay (days)") title("Raw LOS: heavy right skew") ///
    name(d1, replace)
histogram lnlos, fcolor(midblue%40) lcolor(white) ///
    xtitle("log length of stay") title("log LOS: roughly symmetric") ///
    name(d2, replace)
graph combine d1 d2, rows(1)
qui graph export img/rhc_dist.png, replace width(1600)

By disease category. Sepsis and acute respiratory failure longer; CHF and the cancer shorter. Disease category clearly belongs in the model. (by_disease)

graph hbox los, over(cat1, sort(1)) nooutside ///
    title("LOS varies a lot by disease category")
qui graph export img/rhc_cat.png, replace width(1400)
table cat1, statistic(count los) statistic(median los) statistic(mean los)

Some of the short-stay diagnoses are puzzling — hold that thought for section 3.

By disposition and DNR. LOS mixes distinct care trajectories: patients who die in hospital and patients made DNR on day 1 have markedly shorter stays. (by_dnr_died)

twoway (kdensity los if diedhosp==0, lcolor(navy)) ///
       (kdensity los if diedhosp==1, lcolor(cranberry)), ///
       legend(order(1 "Discharged alive" 2 "Died in hospital") ring(0) pos(2)) ///
       xtitle("length of stay") title("LOS mixes survivors and deaths") ///
       name(g1, replace)
twoway (kdensity los if dnr1==0, lcolor(navy)) ///
       (kdensity los if dnr1==1, lcolor(cranberry)), ///
       legend(order(1 "Not DNR" 2 "DNR day 1") ring(0) pos(2)) ///
       xtitle("length of stay") title("Shorter stays under day-1 DNR") ///
       name(g2, replace)
graph combine g1 g2, rows(1)
qui graph export img/rhc_groups.png, replace width(1600)

Across the severity range — the key graph. Pooled, LOS traces an inverted-U in predicted survival. Split by disposition, it is two opposite trends: among survivors, sicker patients stay longer; among those who die, the predicted-to-survive linger longest. The pooled curve is a mixture. (across_sev)

twoway (lowess los surv2md1, lcolor(black) lwidth(thick) lpattern(dash)) ///
       (lowess los surv2md1 if diedhosp==0, lcolor(navy) lwidth(thick)) ///
       (lowess los surv2md1 if diedhosp==1, lcolor(cranberry) lwidth(thick)), ///
       legend(order(1 "All patients (pooled)" 2 "Discharged alive" ///
                    3 "Died in hospital") ring(0) pos(1) cols(1)) ///
       xtitle("Predicted 2-month survival at day 1") ytitle("LOS (days)") ///
       title("The pooled inverted-U is a mixture of two opposite trends")
qui graph export img/rhc_mix.png, replace width(1500)

What did we learn:

  1. describe LOS on the log scale;
  2. include disease category and DNR
  3. allow curvature across the predicted-survival range;
  4. LOS mixes survivors and in-hospital deaths, whose severity patterns run in opposite directions
  5. DNR may account for some of this in the multivariable model;
  6. DNR may explain some of the odd short-stay diagnosis specific LOS.

3. A descriptive model and predictive comparisons

  • Question
  • Hint
  • Answer-1
  • Answer-2
  • Answer-3
  • Answer-4
  • Answer-5

Build the models the graphs suggested:

  1. log outcome, disease category, a curve in predicted survival, and DNR

Because the outcome is logged, how do we talk about days? We want to report predicted mean LOS across disease category, DNR, the survival range, and age. (see Hint)

  1. Display Predicted mean LOS by disease category (case-mix held fixed)
  2. Does DNR explain the odd short-stay diagnoses?
  3. Predicted mean LOS by DNR status and across the survival range
  4. Predicted mean LOS across age

Duan’s (1983) smearing factor Used famously in the Rand Health Insurance Experiment

  • If in prediction you just use exp(xb) - it back-transforms the log LOS to the median, not the mean, because averaging happened on the log scale.
  • The Duan smearing factor: scalar duan = mean(exp(residual)), rescales predictions to the mean.
  • You can include it in the margins command to get predictions in days: margins cat1, expression(duan*exp(xb())).

Fit the new model and build the Duan factor (round2):

regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
capture drop e_resid e_expresid
predict double e_resid, residuals
generate double e_expresid = exp(e_resid)
summarize e_expresid, meanonly
scalar duan = r(mean)
display "Duan smearing factor = " duan

Predicted mean LOS by disease category (case-mix held fixed pr_by_dz):

margins cat1, expression(duan*exp(xb()))
marginsplot, horizontal recast(scatter) ///
    title("Predicted mean LOS by disease category") ///
    xtitle("Predicted LOS (days)")
qui graph export img/rhc_pc_cat.png, replace width(1400)

Does DNR explain the odd short-stay diagnoses? Let DNR interact with disease category. (dnr_by_dz)

quietly regress lnlos i.cat1##i.dnr1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 c.age i.sex
testparm i.cat1#i.dnr1
estimates store m_interact
quietly regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex

Predicted mean LOS by DNR status and across the survival range: (pr_dnr_surv)

margins dnr1, expression(duan*exp(xb()))
marginsplot, recast(scatter) ///
    title("Predicted mean LOS: DNR vs not") ytitle("Predicted LOS (days)")
qui graph export img/rhc_pc_dnr.png, replace width(1300)
margins, at(surv2md1=(0.1(0.05)0.9)) expression(duan*exp(xb()))
marginsplot, recast(line) recastci(rarea) ciopts(color(%20)) ///
    title("Predicted mean LOS across the severity range (an inverted-U)") ///
    ytitle("Predicted LOS (days)") xtitle("Predicted 2-month survival")
qui graph export img/rhc_pc_surv.png, replace width(1400)

Predicted mean LOS across age: (pr_los_age)

margins, at(age=(30(10)90)) expression(duan*exp(xb()))
marginsplot, recast(line) recastci(rarea) ciopts(color(%20)) ///
    title("Predicted mean LOS across age") ytitle("Predicted LOS (days)")
qui graph export img/rhc_pc_age.png, replace width(1400)

These are predictive comparisons — expected stay for patients who share these characteristics, case-mix held fixed — not causal effects of the disease, age, or DNR order itself.

4. The inverted-U is a mixture and a caution about colliders

  • Question
  • Hint
  • Answer

The survival-range prediction (answer A-4 above) again showed the inverted-U, this time while holding other variables constant: expected stay rises, then falls, as day-1 predicted survival increases. It is obvious to most clinicians why the sickest and the healthiest patients have shorter stays.

  1. Show the different survival curves by whether the patient lived or died in the hospital

  2. Given the findings should we simply adjust for in-hospital death to describe the curves better?

Split the curve by whether the patient died in hospital. Then think carefully about when death is measured relative to the day-1 predictors.

Run surv_by_dispo

quietly regress lnlos c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1##i.diedhosp
margins diedhosp, at(surv2md1=(0.1(0.05)0.9)) expression(exp(xb()))
marginsplot, recast(line) ///
    title("Two trajectories: survivors vs in-hospital deaths") ///
    ytitle("Predicted median LOS (days)") xtitle("Predicted 2-month survival")
qui graph export img/rhc_pc_split.png, replace width(1400)

Whether someone lived or died is an event that occurs after the baseline and so if you were to condition on it, it would be a collider. It can introduce spurious associations between variables when you are trying to describe the predictive comparisons between groups.

Think about the following DAG

  • Descriptive goal → allow the flexibility in the baseline predictor above to describe each group.
  • Causal / explanatory goal → treat death as a competing event (cause-specific or Fine–Gray), or use a multi-state or joint (longitudinal–survival) model.

Take-home: you cannot adjust your way out of a downstream-variable collider by adding it to a regression. Selecting a study population based on a collider functions exactly the same way as trying to adjust for it in the regression.

5. Do the predictions look like the data? Overall fit

  • Question
  • Hint
  • Answer-1
  • Answer-2
  • Answer-3
  • Optional

Now check the model as a whole.

  1. Simulate replication datasets from the fitted model and compare them to the observed data
  2. Check pointwise calibration with the PIT and with 50% / 90% interval coverage.
  3. Contrast the naive raw-days model with the log model.
  • Replications: xb + rnormal(0, e(rmse)), overlaid kdensity vs. observed.
  • PIT: Transform the residuals into how many standard deviations they are from the predicted mean and then calculate the probability using the cumulative distribution: normal((y - xb)/rmse). These probabilities should have a uniform, e.g flat, distribution if the pointwise predictive distributions are calibrated.
  • Coverage: the fraction of observations inside xb ± invnormal(p)*rmse should match the nominal 50% / 90% based on how many standard deviations of the error term they are from the predicdtion.

Note: PIT stands for the ugly sounding “probability integral transformation” but just means that you transform the observed data point to the cumulative probability given the conditional mean and standard distribution.

Raw-days model — replications invent negative stays, the PIT is not flat, and the intervals over-cover (p5a1_raw_days):

quietly regress los i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
predict xb_raw, xb
local rmse_raw = e(rmse)
set seed 20260912
local call ""
forvalues i = 1/20 {
    quietly generate los_rep`i' = xb_raw + rnormal(0, `rmse_raw')
    local call `call' (kdensity los_rep`i', lcolor(gs13) lwidth(vthin))
}
twoway `call' (kdensity los, lcolor(navy) lwidth(thick)), legend(off) ///
    xline(0, lpattern(dash) lcolor(red)) xtitle("Length of stay (days)") ///
    title("Raw-days model: replications invent negative stays")
qui graph export img/rhc_ppc_raw.png, replace width(1400)

generate pit_raw = normal((los - xb_raw)/`rmse_raw')
foreach lev in 50 90 {
    local lo = (100 - `lev')/200
    local hi = 1 - `lo'
    quietly count if inrange(los, xb_raw + invnormal(`lo')*`rmse_raw', ///
                                  xb_raw + invnormal(`hi')*`rmse_raw')
    display "RAW coverage of central " `lev' "% = " %4.1f 100*r(N)/_N "% (nominal " `lev' "%)"
}
histogram pit_raw, width(0.05) percent fcolor(midblue%50) lcolor(white) ///
    yline(5, lpattern(dash) lcolor(red)) xtitle("PIT value") ///
    title("Raw model: PIT not flat -> miscalibrated")
qui graph export img/rhc_pit_raw.png, replace width(1300)

Log model — replications track the data, the PIT is much flatter, and coverage lands near nominal (p5a2_lnlos_days):

quietly regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
predict xb_log, xb
local rmse_log = e(rmse)
set seed 20260912
local call ""
forvalues i = 1/20 {
    quietly generate lnlos_rep`i' = xb_log + rnormal(0, `rmse_log')
    local call `call' (kdensity lnlos_rep`i', lcolor(gs13) lwidth(vthin))
}
twoway `call' (kdensity lnlos, lcolor(navy) lwidth(thick)), legend(off) ///
    xtitle("log length of stay") title("log model: replications track the data")
qui graph export img/rhc_ppc_log.png, replace width(1400)

generate pit_log = normal((lnlos - xb_log)/`rmse_log')
foreach lev in 50 90 {
    local lo = (100 - `lev')/200
    local hi = 1 - `lo'
    quietly count if inrange(lnlos, xb_log + invnormal(`lo')*`rmse_log', ///
                                    xb_log + invnormal(`hi')*`rmse_log')
    display "LOG coverage of central " `lev' "% = " %4.1f 100*r(N)/_N "% (nominal " `lev' "%)"
}
histogram pit_log, width(0.05) percent fcolor(midblue%50) lcolor(white) ///
    yline(5, lpattern(dash) lcolor(red)) xtitle("PIT value") ///
    title("log model: PIT much flatter -> calibrated")
qui graph export img/rhc_pit_log.png, replace width(1300)

A caveat for this cacluation of the PIT: normal((y - xb)/rmse) treats the fitted mean xb and the scale rmse as the true parameters, so it is only asymptotically Uniform(0,1). It ignores that xb was fit to y itself and that σ was estimated. The exact finite-sample version can be obtained using a Student-t distribution via the jacknife (deleted) residual — see the optional tab.

Model-comparison. Coverage being a probability, is comparable across the raw and log scales (unlike AIC, which is not comparable across a transformed outcome) (p5a3_model_comp):

quietly regress los i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
quietly predict double xbr, xb
local rr = e(rmse)
quietly count if xbr < 0
scalar neg_raw = r(N)
qui foreach lev in 50 90 {
    local lo = (100 - `lev')/200
    local hi = 1 - `lo'
    quietly count if inrange(los, xbr + invnormal(`lo')*`rr', xbr + invnormal(`hi')*`rr')
    scalar cov`lev'_raw = 100*r(N)/_N
}
quietly regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
quietly predict double xbl, xb
local rl = e(rmse)
qui foreach lev in 50 90 {
    local lo = (100 - `lev')/200
    local hi = 1 - `lo'
    quietly count if inrange(lnlos, xbl + invnormal(`lo')*`rl', xbl + invnormal(`hi')*`rl')
    scalar cov`lev'_log = 100*r(N)/_N
}
display "                              naive RAW-days      final LOG model"
display "impossible (<0) predictions  " %8.0f neg_raw  "            " %8.0f 0
display "50% interval coverage        " %7.1f cov50_raw "%           " %7.1f cov50_log "%"
display "90% interval coverage        " %7.1f cov90_raw "%           " %7.1f cov90_log "%"
                              naive RAW-days      final LOG model

impossible (<0) predictions         5                   0

50% interval coverage           73.0%              50.9%

90% interval coverage           94.7%              89.2%

On the log scale the simulated datasets resemble the real data and the pointwise intervals cover near their nominal rates unlike the raw-days model.

Exact PIT (parameter uncertainty)

The plug-in PIT above is only asymptotically uniform. The problem is that patient i’s own data helped fit the line, so the line is pulled toward the observed \(y_i\), which means the residual is artificially small, especially for unusual patients. This can result in underdispersed residuals and a PIT graph that instead of being flat is bumped up in the middle.

Under a correctly specified normal linear model the exactly uniform quantity is found using the externally studentized (deleted) residual

\[t_i=\frac{e_i}{s_{(i)}\sqrt{1-h_{ii}}}\sim t_{\,n-p-1},\qquad u_i=T_{n-p-1}(t_i)\sim\text{Uniform}(0,1).\]

That \(t_i\) is the standardized leave-one-out prediction error (\(y_i-\hat y_{i(i)}=e_i/(1-h_{ii})\), with LOO (leave out one) variance \(s_{(i)}^2/(1-h_{ii})\)). In common language this quantifies how surprising is this specific patient’s stay, in standard deviations, compared to a prediction and an error spread both computed without this patient’s observation.

This form of the PIT is the frequentist predictive distribution that includes parameter uncertainty — the exact analog of the Bayesian posterior-predictive PIT. In Stata it is obtained using: predict t, rstudent then 1 - ttail(e(df_r)-1, t).

* Exact deleted-residual PIT, raw model
quietly regress los i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
scalar df_t = e(df_r) - 1
predict double rstud_raw, rstudent
generate double pit_raw_exact = 1 - ttail(df_t, rstud_raw)
histogram pit_raw_exact, width(0.05) percent fcolor(midblue%50) lcolor(white) ///
    yline(5, lpattern(dash) lcolor(red)) xtitle("exact PIT") ///
    title("Raw model: still not flat") name(pe_raw, replace)
* Exact deleted-residual PIT, log model
quietly regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
scalar df_t = e(df_r) - 1
predict double rstud_log, rstudent
generate double pit_log_exact = 1 - ttail(df_t, rstud_log)
histogram pit_log_exact, width(0.05) percent fcolor(midblue%50) lcolor(white) ///
    yline(5, lpattern(dash) lcolor(red)) xtitle("exact PIT") ///
    title("log model: flat") name(pe_log, replace)
graph combine pe_raw pe_log, rows(1)
qui graph export img/rhc_pit_exact.png, replace width(1600)

The exact PIT gives the same verdict and, with n ≈ 5700 and tiny leverage (\(h_{ii}\approx p/n\approx 0.003\), so \(t_{n-p-1}\approx\) normal), is numerically almost indistinguishable from the plug-in here. The raw model stays non-uniform because the main problem is the outcome shape not the plug-in approximation.

6. Checking the assumptions, in severity order

  • Question
  • Hint
  • Answer-1
  • Answer-2
  • Answer-3
  • Answer-4
  • Answer-5

Now, after all that, the textbook checks. The chapter orders them by the severity of their consequences:

  1. correct functional form — biases coefficients;
  2. endogeneity (predictors correlated with the error) — biases coefficients;
  3. independent errors — affects standard errors;
  4. homoskedasticity — affects standard errors;
  5. normal errors — affects standard errors, least consequential.

Which of these actually matter for this LOS model?

Functional form: acprplot, estat ovtest (RESET), and AIC/BIC for the quadratic term. Endogeneity: there is no command — argue it with a DAG. Independence: cluster the SEs. Homoskedasticity: rvfplot and a robust-SE safety net. Normality: qnorm.

1. Functional form. Confirm the curvature modeled in surv2md1, and check the quadratic (p6a1_fnxn):

quietly regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
capture noisily acprplot surv2md1, lowess lsopts(lcolor(cranberry)) ///
    title("Component-plus-residual: surv2md1 (linear fit)")
qui graph export img/rhc_ff_acpr.png, replace width(1400)
estat ovtest
estimates store ff_linear
quietly regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
estimates store ff_quad
estimates stats ff_linear ff_quad
Ramsey RESET test for omitted variables
Omitted: Powers of fitted values of lnlos

H0: Model has no omitted variables

F(3, 5718) =   3.16
  Prob > F = 0.0237





Akaike's information criterion and Bayesian information criterion

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
       Model |          N   ll(null)  ll(model)      df        AIC        BIC
-------------+---------------------------------------------------------------
   ff_linear |      5,734  -7706.042  -7419.037      13   14864.07   14950.58
     ff_quad |      5,734  -7706.042  -7382.425      14   14792.85   14886.01
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Note: BIC uses N = number of observations. See [R] IC note.

The Ramsey test suggests that there is an omitted variable or a non-linear relationship.

The AIC and BIC suggest that the model with the quadratic fits better than the one without.

2. Endogeneity. There is rarely any way to check this from the data. OLS forces the fitted residuals to be mechanically uncorrelated with the predictors, so an omitted baseline confounder hides inside the (biased) coefficients, not in a residual plot. Satisfying the assumption can only be argued by design and theory — supported by a DAG drawn before fitting.

There are some procedures for looking at how senstive your coefficients would be to an umeasured confounder (Oster/coefficient-stability sensitivity (psacalc)). If you can think of a variable that effectively randomizes an exposure in the model then you can use this as an instrument and test using a Hausman test (ivregress 2sls then estat endog).

As we pointed out in section 4: conditioning on in-hospital death by only analyzing survivors is endogenous selection — you cannot adjust your way out of endogeneity by adding a downstream variable.

3. Independent errors. (p6a3_indep) Think about potential clustering of data. For example, you could examine clustering within disease category (different diseases may have shared teams, protocols, pathways). Compare default and diagnosis-clustered SEs:

quietly regress lnlos c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex i.cat1
estimates store se_default
quietly regress lnlos c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex i.cat1, vce(cluster cat1)
estimates store se_cluster
estimates table se_default se_cluster, keep(1.dnr1 age) b(%6.3f) se ///
title("Default vs. diagnosis-clustered standard errors")
Default vs. diagnosis-clustered standard errors

----------------------------------
    Variable | se_de~t   se_cl~r  
-------------+--------------------
        dnr1 |
        yes  |  -0.588    -0.588  
             |   0.038     0.066  
         age |  -0.003    -0.003  
             |   0.001     0.001  
----------------------------------
                      Legend: b/se

4. Homoskedasticity. (p6a4_hetero)

On the chosen log model the residual spread is roughly even across fitted values (section 5 already showed the raw-days model fails badly); you can add robust-SE to be sure that the standard errors are not under-estimated if there is any residual heteroskedasticity:

quietly regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
rvfplot, yline(0) title("log LOS: residual spread roughly even")
qui graph export img/rhc_rvf_log.png, replace width(1400)
estimates store hs_default
quietly regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex, vce(robust)
estimates store hs_robust
estimates table hs_default hs_robust, keep(1.dnr1 age) b(%6.3f) se ///
    title("Default vs. heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors")
NA
Default vs. heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors

----------------------------------
    Variable | hs_de~t   hs_ro~t  
-------------+--------------------
        dnr1 |
        yes  |  -0.588    -0.588  
             |   0.038     0.038  
         age |  -0.003    -0.003  
             |   0.001     0.001  
----------------------------------
                      Legend: b/se

5. Normal errors — the least consequential check (p6a5_normal):

quietly regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
predict r_log, resid
qnorm r_log, title("log LOS residuals: close to normal")
qui graph export img/rhc_qq_log.png, replace width(1400)

With n ≈ 5700 the CLT already protects the predictive comparisons, so normality was the least consequential check.

7. Epilog: use Poisson instead of log-OLS

  • Question
  • Hint
  • Answer

All the retransformation fuss in section 3 exists only because we logged the outcome. Is there a model that gives mean days directly, with no smearing factor?

Poisson regression puts the log on the link, modeling E(LOS|X) = exp(Xβ) on the day scale. With vce(robust) the Poisson pseudo-MLE is consistent for that mean even though LOS is not a count and is over-dispersed (Gould 2011; Silva & Tenreyro 2006).

poisson los i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex, vce(robust)
margins cat1
marginsplot, horizontal recast(scatter) ///
    title("Poisson: predicted mean LOS by disease category") ///
    xtitle("Predicted LOS (days)")
qui graph export img/rhc_pois_cat.png, replace width(1400)

Side-by-side, the two methods for getting a mean on the day scale — log-OLS + Duan smearing, and Poisson with robust SEs — reach a similar place:

quietly regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
capture drop er2 eer2
predict double er2, residuals
generate double eer2 = exp(er2)
summarize eer2, meanonly
scalar duan2 = r(mean)
quietly margins cat1, expression(duan2*exp(xb())) post
estimates store logols_duan
quietly poisson los i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex, vce(robust)
quietly margins cat1, post
estimates store poisson_mean
estimates table logols_duan poisson_mean, b(%6.2f) se ///
    title("Predicted mean LOS by disease category: log-OLS+Duan vs Poisson")
Predicted mean LOS by disease category: log-OLS+Duan vs Poisson

----------------------------------
    Variable | logol~n   poiss~n  
-------------+--------------------
        cat1 |
        ARF  |   22.76     22.47  
             |    0.40      0.49  
       COPD  |   20.82     20.60  
             |    0.93      1.28  
        CHF  |   15.54     15.54  
             |    0.74      0.99  
  Cirrhosis  |   15.94     14.58  
             |    0.94      0.99  
       Coma  |   16.56     17.53  
             |    0.76      1.05  
Colon Can..  |    8.76      6.80  
             |    2.91      2.00  
Lung Cancer  |   11.38      9.32  
             |    1.60      1.01  
MOSF w/Ma..  |   18.06     16.32  
             |    0.88      0.84  
MOSF w/Se..  |   24.99     26.42  
             |    0.63      0.88  
----------------------------------
                      Legend: b/se

The Poisson route needs no retransformation and carries its own robust standard errors — so for a skewed, positive outcome like LOS, you can use poisson rather than regress.

Recap:

In the end, we did not check the model to certify it afterword; we checked it as part of building it. In order of consequence:

  • Outcome scale (sections 1, 2, 5): a naive normal-error model on raw days predicts impossible negative stays and is miscalibrated. Logging fixes both.
  • A hidden mixture (sections 2, 4): the inverted-U in predicted survival is survivors and deaths running in opposite directions — you can describe them separately, but do not “adjust” for a downstream collider.
  • Confounding by design (section 6, endogeneity): this problem can not be identifed in model checking it has to be argued
  • Standard-error assumptions (section 6): independence, homoskedasticity, normality — the least consequential, and largely handled by the log scale, cluster or robust SEs, and a large enough sample.

```{stata, collectcode=TRUE, echo=FALSE, results="hide"}
*| eval: true
capture set scheme burd
use rhc_class_tph.dta, clear
generate los = dschdte - sadmdte
label variable los "Hospital length of stay (days)"
drop if missing(los) | los <= 0
generate lnlos = ln(los)
label variable lnlos "log length of stay"
* In-hospital disposition: death date on or before discharge date.
generate byte diedhosp = !missing(dthdte) & dthdte <= dschdte
label define disp 0 "Discharged alive" 1 "Died in hospital"
label values diedhosp disp
label variable diedhosp "In-hospital disposition"
* Canonical descriptive model + Duan smearing factor, shared by the sections below.
regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
predict double e_resid, residuals
generate double e_expresid = exp(e_resid)
summarize e_expresid, meanonly
scalar duan = r(mean)
```

## Support study

* SUPPORT trial 1989-1994 tested an intervention to improve end-of-life decision making and reduce mechanically supported, painful, and prolonged process of dying.
* Intervention: Physicians and their seriously ill admitted patients were randomized at the physician level to receiving daily estimates of 6 month survival for each patient and nursing support to work on a) eliciting preferences, b) helping family understand predicted outcomes, c) facilitate advanced plannng and d) communication. 
<!-- massive academic teaching hospitals over a two-year period, hundreds of rotating residents, fellows, and attending physicians passed through these randomized specialty services. The exact number of individual physicians shifted continuously as medical staff rotated onto the services.investigators analyzed the patient-level outcomes (such as 30-day mortality, ICU days, and DNR timing) using standard individual-level regressions and survival analyses without adjusting for the clustering effect, in SUPPORT's case, the intervention failed so completely to show an effect (small effects overlapping CI) that a cluster-adjusted analysis would not have changed the final conclusions-->
* Design: 2-year prospective observational study (phase I - 4301 patients) then a 2-year clinical trial (phase II) that randomized clinical services or specialty groups with their patients (2652-intervention, 2152 control).  (A cluster was defined as a distinct clinical service or subspecialty group at a hospital, e.g. all the attending physicians and residents assigned to the Cardiology Service, General Internal Medicine Team A, or the Pulmonary/Critical Care Service)

::: {style="height: 250px;"}
:::


### Support/RHC Study
* Emebeded within Support Trial  (Connors et al., 1996) 
* MotivationLevaluate the clinical effectiveness of Right Heart Catheterization (RHC)—also known as a Swan-Ganz catheter—in the initial 24 hours of adult care in the intensive care unit (ICU). 
* RHC was widely used but with little evidence supporting use
* (enough) Clinicians strong belief in the benfit precluded RCT.
* Design: Prospective cohort study. N=5734 patients from the parent SUPPORT study
* Inclusion: 
    * admitted to the ICU in the first 24 hours 
    * fit one of 9 pre-specified diagnostic categories
    * complete covariate data recorded in the first 24 hours.

Load the data (`load_data`)

::: {style="height: 250px;"}
:::


## 1. Model of predictors of length of stay (LOS) {#sec-naive}

<!--
The SUPPORT investigators did not rely solely on the off-the-shelf APACHE III equation because it was primarily built to predict in-hospital mortality, not specific time horizons like 2 months. Instead, they built a custom, disease-specific Cox proportional hazards statistical model. [1] (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1959406/)The aps1 score was fed into that model alongside other critical survival predictors:\(\text{surv2md1}=f(\mathbf{aps1}+\text{scoma1}+\text{age}+\text{primary\ disease\ category}+\text{comorbidities})\)
-->

::: panel-tabset

### Question

We want to describe how hospital length of stay varies across ICU patients. 

* One of the advantages of SUPPORT was the comprehensive severity of illness data summarized in the 2 and 6 month survival prediction.
* Knaus (the APACHE developer) was an investigator and the acute physiology score on day 1 is part of the prediction model.

Fit a model on disease category, day-1 predicted survival, age, and sex (`round1`):

```stata
use rhc_class_tph.dta, clear
generate los = dschdte - sadmdte
drop if missing(los) | los <= 0
regress los i.cat1 c.surv2md1 c.age i.sex
```

The coefficient table looks reasonable and most predictors are "significant" 

**Are we done?**

### Hint

**Try simulating an outcome from the fitted model and compare to the data.** 

A normal-error model spreads predictions *symmetrically* around the mean. 

::: {style="height: 300px;"}
:::

### Answer

Fit the model, then simulate one dataset from it and count how many stays are **negative**:  (replicate `ans_x2d`)

```{stata}
regress los i.cat1 c.surv2md1 c.age i.sex
set seed 20260912
qui predict double xb_naive
generate double los_sim = xb_naive + rnormal(0, e(rmse))
count if los_sim < 0
twoway (kdensity los, lcolor(navy) lwidth(thick)) ///
       (kdensity los_sim, lcolor(cranberry) lwidth(thick)), ///
       xline(0, lpattern(dash) lcolor(red)) ///
       legend(order(1 "Observed LOS" 2 "Simulated from model") ring(0) pos(2)) ///
       xtitle("Length of stay (days)") ///
       title("The model invents impossible negative stays")
qui graph export img/rhc_naive_sim.png, replace width(1400)
```

![Observed length of stay versus a dataset simulated from the naive model. The simulated distribution is symmetric and pushes a large mass below zero (dashed red line), which is impossible for a length of stay.](img/rhc_naive_sim.png){width=70% .lightbox}

More than a thousand simulated patients have a **negative** length of stay. A stay cannot be negative, so the model is already telling us it is the **wrong shape** for this outcome. 


:::



## 2. What does the outcome look like overall and across predictors? 

::: panel-tabset

### Question

Think about functional form and **graph the data**. 

1. What does LOS look like **raw vs. logged**?
2. How does it differ across **primary disease category**?
3. How does it differ by **DNR status** and by **in-hospital death**?
4. How does it change across a **severity range** (day-1 predicted survival)?

::: {style="height: 300px;"}
:::

### Hint

- `histogram` of `los` and of `ln(los)` — is either roughly symmetric?
- `graph hbox` over `cat1` — do the differences make sense?
- `kdensity` by `dnr1` and by `diedhosp` — does LOS mix distinct groups?
- `lowess` of LOS on `surv2md1`, pooled and then split by `diedhosp` — is the pooled shape a single trend or a **mixture**?

::: {style="height: 300px;"}
:::

### Answer-1

**Raw vs. log.** The raw outcome is heavily right-skewed with a floor at zero; the log scale is roughly symmetric. (`raw_vs_log`)

```{stata}
histogram los, width(10) fcolor(midblue%40) lcolor(white) ///
    xtitle("Length of stay (days)") title("Raw LOS: heavy right skew") ///
    name(d1, replace)
histogram lnlos, fcolor(midblue%40) lcolor(white) ///
    xtitle("log length of stay") title("log LOS: roughly symmetric") ///
    name(d2, replace)
graph combine d1 d2, rows(1)
qui graph export img/rhc_dist.png, replace width(1600)
```

![Histograms of raw and log length of stay. Raw LOS is strongly right-skewed with a floor at zero; log LOS is close to symmetric.](img/rhc_dist.png){width=85% .lightbox}

### Answer-2

**By disease category.** Sepsis and acute respiratory failure longer; CHF and the cancer shorter. Disease category clearly belongs in the model. (`by_disease`)

```{stata}
graph hbox los, over(cat1, sort(1)) nooutside ///
    title("LOS varies a lot by disease category")
qui graph export img/rhc_cat.png, replace width(1400)
table cat1, statistic(count los) statistic(median los) statistic(mean los)
```

![Horizontal box plots of LOS by primary disease category, sorted by median. Sepsis and acute respiratory failure have the longest stays; congestive heart failure and cancers the shortest.](img/rhc_cat.png){width=75% .lightbox}

Some of the *short*-stay diagnoses are puzzling — hold that thought for section 3.

### Answer-3

**By disposition and DNR.** LOS mixes distinct care trajectories: patients who die in hospital and patients made DNR on day 1 have markedly shorter stays. (`by_dnr_died`)

```{stata}
twoway (kdensity los if diedhosp==0, lcolor(navy)) ///
       (kdensity los if diedhosp==1, lcolor(cranberry)), ///
       legend(order(1 "Discharged alive" 2 "Died in hospital") ring(0) pos(2)) ///
       xtitle("length of stay") title("LOS mixes survivors and deaths") ///
       name(g1, replace)
twoway (kdensity los if dnr1==0, lcolor(navy)) ///
       (kdensity los if dnr1==1, lcolor(cranberry)), ///
       legend(order(1 "Not DNR" 2 "DNR day 1") ring(0) pos(2)) ///
       xtitle("length of stay") title("Shorter stays under day-1 DNR") ///
       name(g2, replace)
graph combine g1 g2, rows(1)
qui graph export img/rhc_groups.png, replace width(1600)
```

![Kernel densities of LOS by in-hospital death and by day-1 DNR status. Patients who die in hospital, and patients made DNR, have shorter stays.](img/rhc_groups.png){width=85% .lightbox}

### Answer-4

**Across the severity range — the key graph.** Pooled, LOS traces an **inverted-U** in predicted survival. Split by disposition, it is **two opposite trends**: among survivors, sicker patients stay longer; among those who die, the predicted-to-survive linger longest. The pooled curve is a **mixture**. (`across_sev`)

```{stata}
twoway (lowess los surv2md1, lcolor(black) lwidth(thick) lpattern(dash)) ///
       (lowess los surv2md1 if diedhosp==0, lcolor(navy) lwidth(thick)) ///
       (lowess los surv2md1 if diedhosp==1, lcolor(cranberry) lwidth(thick)), ///
       legend(order(1 "All patients (pooled)" 2 "Discharged alive" ///
                    3 "Died in hospital") ring(0) pos(1) cols(1)) ///
       xtitle("Predicted 2-month survival at day 1") ytitle("LOS (days)") ///
       title("The pooled inverted-U is a mixture of two opposite trends")
qui graph export img/rhc_mix.png, replace width(1500)
```

![Lowess curves of LOS against day-1 predicted survival: the pooled curve is an inverted-U, while the curves split by in-hospital death run in opposite directions, showing the pooled shape is a mixture.](img/rhc_mix.png){width=75% .lightbox}

### take-home

**What did we learn:** 

1. describe LOS on the **log scale**; 
2. include **disease category** and **DNR**  
3. allow **curvature** across the predicted-survival range; 
4. LOS **mixes** survivors and in-hospital deaths, whose severity patterns run in opposite directions 
5. DNR may account for some of this in the multivariable model; 
6. DNR may explain some of the odd short-stay diagnosis specific LOS.

::: {style="height: 200px;"}
:::

:::


## 3. A descriptive model and predictive comparisons {#sec-model}

::: panel-tabset

### Question

Build the models the graphs suggested:

1.  log outcome, disease category, a curve in predicted survival, and DNR

Because the outcome is logged, how do we talk about **days**? We want to report predicted **mean** LOS across disease category, DNR, the survival range, and age. (see Hint)

2. Display Predicted mean LOS by disease category (case-mix held fixed)
3. Does DNR explain the odd short-stay diagnoses?
4. Predicted mean LOS by DNR status and across the survival range
5. Predicted mean LOS across age

::: {style="height: 350px;"}
:::

### Hint

**Duan's (1983) smearing factor** Used famously in the Rand Health Insurance Experiment

- If in prediction you just use `exp(xb)` - it back-transforms the log LOS to the **median**, not the mean, because averaging happened on the log scale.
- The Duan smearing factor: `scalar duan = mean(exp(residual))`, rescales predictions to the mean.
- You can include it in the `margins` command to get predictions in days: `margins cat1, expression(duan*exp(xb()))`.

::: {style="height: 400px;"}
:::

### Answer-1

Fit the new model and build the Duan factor (`round2`):

```{stata}
*| eval: true
regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
capture drop e_resid e_expresid
predict double e_resid, residuals
generate double e_expresid = exp(e_resid)
summarize e_expresid, meanonly
scalar duan = r(mean)
display "Duan smearing factor = " duan
```

### Answer-2
**Predicted mean LOS by disease category** (case-mix held fixed `pr_by_dz`):

```{stata}
margins cat1, expression(duan*exp(xb()))
marginsplot, horizontal recast(scatter) ///
    title("Predicted mean LOS by disease category") ///
    xtitle("Predicted LOS (days)")
qui graph export img/rhc_pc_cat.png, replace width(1400)
```

![Predicted mean length of stay by disease category, back-transformed to days with the Duan factor.](img/rhc_pc_cat.png){width=70% .lightbox}

### Answer-3
**Does DNR explain the odd short-stay diagnoses?**  Let DNR interact
with disease category. (`dnr_by_dz`)

```{stata}
*| eval: true
quietly regress lnlos i.cat1##i.dnr1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 c.age i.sex
testparm i.cat1#i.dnr1
estimates store m_interact
quietly regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
estimates store m_additive
estimates stats m_additive m_interact
```

```{stata echo=2:4}
*| eval: false
quietly regress lnlos i.cat1##i.dnr1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 c.age i.sex
qui margins cat1#dnr1, expression(duan*exp(xb()))
marginsplot, recast(scatter) xlabel(, angle(45))
qui graph export img/dnr_by_dz.png, replace width(1400)
```

![Predicted mean length of stay by disease category and DNR, back-transformed to days with the Duan factor.](img/dnr_by_dz.png){width=100% .lightbox}

### Answer-4
**Predicted mean LOS by DNR status** and **across the survival range**: (`pr_dnr_surv`)

```{stata}
*| eval: false
margins dnr1, expression(duan*exp(xb()))
marginsplot, recast(scatter) ///
    title("Predicted mean LOS: DNR vs not") ytitle("Predicted LOS (days)")
qui graph export img/rhc_pc_dnr.png, replace width(1300)
```

![Predicted mean LOS for DNR versus non-DNR patients.](img/rhc_pc_dnr.png){width=60% .lightbox}

```{stata}
*| eval: false
margins, at(surv2md1=(0.1(0.05)0.9)) expression(duan*exp(xb()))
marginsplot, recast(line) recastci(rarea) ciopts(color(%20)) ///
    title("Predicted mean LOS across the severity range (an inverted-U)") ///
    ytitle("Predicted LOS (days)") xtitle("Predicted 2-month survival")
qui graph export img/rhc_pc_surv.png, replace width(1400)
```

![Predicted mean LOS across the day-1 predicted-survival range, showing an inverted-U.](img/rhc_pc_surv.png){width=70% .lightbox}

### Answer-5
**Predicted mean LOS across age:** (`pr_los_age`)

```{stata}
margins, at(age=(30(10)90)) expression(duan*exp(xb()))
marginsplot, recast(line) recastci(rarea) ciopts(color(%20)) ///
    title("Predicted mean LOS across age") ytitle("Predicted LOS (days)")
qui graph export img/rhc_pc_age.png, replace width(1400)
```

![Predicted mean LOS across age.](img/rhc_pc_age.png){width=70%}

These are **predictive comparisons** — expected stay for patients who share these
characteristics, case-mix held fixed — **not** causal effects of the disease, age, or DNR
order itself.

:::



## 4. The inverted-U is a mixture and a caution about colliders  {#sec-collider}

::: panel-tabset

### Question

The survival-range prediction (answer A-4 above) again showed the **inverted-U**, this time while holding other variables constant: expected stay rises, then falls, as day-1 predicted survival increases. It is obvious to most clinicians why the sickest and the healthiest patients have shorter stays.

1. Show the different survival curves by whether the patient lived or died in the hospital

2. Given the findings should we simply **adjust** for in-hospital death to describe the curves better?

::: {style="height: 500px;"}
:::

### Hint

Split the curve by whether the patient **died in hospital**. Then think carefully about *when* death is measured relative to the day-1 predictors.

::: {style="height: 500px;"}
:::

### Answer

Run `surv_by_dispo`

```{stata}
quietly regress lnlos c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1##i.diedhosp
margins diedhosp, at(surv2md1=(0.1(0.05)0.9)) expression(exp(xb()))
marginsplot, recast(line) ///
    title("Two trajectories: survivors vs in-hospital deaths") ///
    ytitle("Predicted median LOS (days)") xtitle("Predicted 2-month survival")
qui graph export img/rhc_pc_split.png, replace width(1400)
```

![Predicted LOS across the survival range, split by in-hospital death: survivors and deaths run in opposite directions, explaining the pooled inverted-U.](img/rhc_pc_split.png){width=70% .lightbox}

Whether someone lived or died is an event that occurs *after* the baseline and so if you were to condition on it, it would be a *collider*.  It can introduce spurious associations between variables when you are trying to describe the predictive comparisons between groups.

Think about the following DAG

::: {#fig-dot-graphs layout-ncol=2 fig-cap="*(a)* Based on prior knowledge and biologic plausibility we propose that there is no causal relationship between attractiveness and acting talent (@Pearl_2018 p 115) *(b)* Conditioning on a common outcome of the primary predictor and outcome (actor status in this case), by sample restriction to status of being an actor, induces a relationship between attractiveness and talent even when there is no causal relationship"}
```{dot}
//| label: fig-dag-collider1
//| eval: true
//| fig-height: 1.5
//| fig-width: 3
digraph {
  graph [ranksep = 0.2]
  node [shape = plaintext]
    X [label = "Ball Skill"]
    Y [label = "Height"]
    C [label = "pro-Basketball player"]
  edge [minlen = 3]
    X->C
    Y->C
  { rank = same; X; Y }
}
```
```{dot}
//| label: fig-dag-collider2
//| eval: true
//| fig-height: 1.5
//| fig-width: 3
digraph {
  graph [ranksep = 0.2]
  node [shape = plaintext]
    X [label = "Ball Skill"]
    Y [label = "Height"]
    C [label = "Pro-basketball player",shape=box]
  edge [minlen = 3]
    X->C
    Y->C
    X->Y [style=dashed, arrowhead=none]
  { rank = same; X; Y }
}
```

If you select based on being a professional basketball player, even if height and ball skill are independent of each other you will have a population that have negative correlation between the two.  Can you draw a figure to show why?

:::

- **Descriptive** goal → allow the flexibility in the baseline predictor above to describe each group.
- **Causal / explanatory** goal → treat death as a **competing event** (cause-specific or Fine–Gray), or use a **multi-state** or **joint** (longitudinal–survival) model.


Take-home: you cannot adjust your way out of a downstream-variable collider by adding it to a regression.  Selecting a study population based on a collider functions exactly the same way as trying to adjust for it in the regression.

:::

## 5. Do the predictions look like the data? Overall fit {#sec-overall}

::: panel-tabset

### Question

Now check the model as a whole.

1. Simulate replication datasets from the fitted model and compare them to the observed data 
2. Check pointwise calibration with the **PIT** and with **50% / 90% interval coverage**. 
3. Contrast the naive **raw-days** model with the **log** model.

::: {style="height: 500px;"}
:::

### Hint

- Replications: `xb + rnormal(0, e(rmse))`, overlaid `kdensity` vs. observed.
- **PIT**: Transform the residuals into how many standard deviations they are from the predicted mean and then calculate the probability using the cumulative distribution: `normal((y - xb)/rmse)`. These probabilities should have a uniform, e.g **flat**, distribution if the pointwise predictive distributions are calibrated.
- **Coverage**: the fraction of observations inside `xb ± invnormal(p)*rmse` should match the nominal 50% / 90% based on how many standard deviations of the error term they are from the predicdtion.

Note: PIT stands for the ugly sounding "probability integral transformation" but just means that you transform the observed data point to the cumulative probability given the conditional mean and standard distribution.

::: {style="height: 400px;"}
:::

### Answer-1

**Raw-days model** — replications invent negative stays, the PIT is not flat, and the
intervals over-cover (`p5a1_raw_days`):

```{stata}
quietly regress los i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
predict xb_raw, xb
local rmse_raw = e(rmse)
set seed 20260912
local call ""
forvalues i = 1/20 {
    quietly generate los_rep`i' = xb_raw + rnormal(0, `rmse_raw')
    local call `call' (kdensity los_rep`i', lcolor(gs13) lwidth(vthin))
}
twoway `call' (kdensity los, lcolor(navy) lwidth(thick)), legend(off) ///
    xline(0, lpattern(dash) lcolor(red)) xtitle("Length of stay (days)") ///
    title("Raw-days model: replications invent negative stays")
qui graph export img/rhc_ppc_raw.png, replace width(1400)

generate pit_raw = normal((los - xb_raw)/`rmse_raw')
foreach lev in 50 90 {
    local lo = (100 - `lev')/200
    local hi = 1 - `lo'
    quietly count if inrange(los, xb_raw + invnormal(`lo')*`rmse_raw', ///
                                  xb_raw + invnormal(`hi')*`rmse_raw')
    display "RAW coverage of central " `lev' "% = " %4.1f 100*r(N)/_N "% (nominal " `lev' "%)"
}
histogram pit_raw, width(0.05) percent fcolor(midblue%50) lcolor(white) ///
    yline(5, lpattern(dash) lcolor(red)) xtitle("PIT value") ///
    title("Raw model: PIT not flat -> miscalibrated")
qui graph export img/rhc_pit_raw.png, replace width(1300)
```

![Twenty replication densities from the raw-days model overlaid on the observed LOS; the replications spread below zero.](img/rhc_ppc_raw.png){width=70% .lightbox}

![PIT histogram for the raw-days model: far from flat, indicating miscalibration.](img/rhc_pit_raw.png){width=60% .lightbox}

### Answer-2

**Log model** — replications track the data, the PIT is much flatter, and coverage lands
near nominal (`p5a2_lnlos_days`):

```{stata}
quietly regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
predict xb_log, xb
local rmse_log = e(rmse)
set seed 20260912
local call ""
forvalues i = 1/20 {
    quietly generate lnlos_rep`i' = xb_log + rnormal(0, `rmse_log')
    local call `call' (kdensity lnlos_rep`i', lcolor(gs13) lwidth(vthin))
}
twoway `call' (kdensity lnlos, lcolor(navy) lwidth(thick)), legend(off) ///
    xtitle("log length of stay") title("log model: replications track the data")
qui graph export img/rhc_ppc_log.png, replace width(1400)

generate pit_log = normal((lnlos - xb_log)/`rmse_log')
foreach lev in 50 90 {
    local lo = (100 - `lev')/200
    local hi = 1 - `lo'
    quietly count if inrange(lnlos, xb_log + invnormal(`lo')*`rmse_log', ///
                                    xb_log + invnormal(`hi')*`rmse_log')
    display "LOG coverage of central " `lev' "% = " %4.1f 100*r(N)/_N "% (nominal " `lev' "%)"
}
histogram pit_log, width(0.05) percent fcolor(midblue%50) lcolor(white) ///
    yline(5, lpattern(dash) lcolor(red)) xtitle("PIT value") ///
    title("log model: PIT much flatter -> calibrated")
qui graph export img/rhc_pit_log.png, replace width(1300)
```

![Twenty replication densities from the log model overlaid on observed log LOS; the replications track the data closely.](img/rhc_ppc_log.png){width=70% .lightbox}

![PIT histogram for the log model: much closer to flat.](img/rhc_pit_log.png){width=60% .lightbox}

A caveat for this cacluation of the PIT: `normal((y - xb)/rmse)` treats the fitted mean `xb` and the scale `rmse` as the *true* parameters, so it is only **asymptotically** Uniform(0,1). It ignores that `xb` was fit to `y` itself and that σ was estimated. The exact finite-sample version can be obtained using a Student-t distribution  via the jacknife (deleted) residual — see the optional tab.

### Answer-3

**Model-comparison.** Coverage being a probability, is comparable across the
raw and log scales (unlike AIC, which is not comparable across a transformed outcome) (`p5a3_model_comp`):

```{stata}
*| eval: true
quietly regress los i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
quietly predict double xbr, xb
local rr = e(rmse)
quietly count if xbr < 0
scalar neg_raw = r(N)
qui foreach lev in 50 90 {
    local lo = (100 - `lev')/200
    local hi = 1 - `lo'
    quietly count if inrange(los, xbr + invnormal(`lo')*`rr', xbr + invnormal(`hi')*`rr')
    scalar cov`lev'_raw = 100*r(N)/_N
}
quietly regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
quietly predict double xbl, xb
local rl = e(rmse)
qui foreach lev in 50 90 {
    local lo = (100 - `lev')/200
    local hi = 1 - `lo'
    quietly count if inrange(lnlos, xbl + invnormal(`lo')*`rl', xbl + invnormal(`hi')*`rl')
    scalar cov`lev'_log = 100*r(N)/_N
}
display "                              naive RAW-days      final LOG model"
display "impossible (<0) predictions  " %8.0f neg_raw  "            " %8.0f 0
display "50% interval coverage        " %7.1f cov50_raw "%           " %7.1f cov50_log "%"
display "90% interval coverage        " %7.1f cov90_raw "%           " %7.1f cov90_log "%"
```

On the log scale the simulated datasets resemble the real data and the pointwise
intervals cover near their nominal rates unlike the raw-days model.

### Optional

**Exact PIT (parameter uncertainty)**

The plug-in PIT above is only asymptotically uniform.  The problem is that patient i's own data helped fit the line, so the line is pulled toward the observed $y_i$, which means the residual is artificially small, especially for unusual patients.  This can result in underdispersed residuals and a PIT graph that instead of being flat is bumped up in the middle.

Under a correctly specified normal linear model the **exactly** uniform quantity is found using the *externally studentized (deleted) residual*

$$t_i=\frac{e_i}{s_{(i)}\sqrt{1-h_{ii}}}\sim t_{\,n-p-1},\qquad u_i=T_{n-p-1}(t_i)\sim\text{Uniform}(0,1).$$

That $t_i$ is the standardized **leave-one-out** prediction error ($y_i-\hat y_{i(i)}=e_i/(1-h_{ii})$, with LOO (leave out one) variance $s_{(i)}^2/(1-h_{ii})$).  In common language this quantifies how surprising is this specific patient's stay, in standard deviations, compared to a prediction and an error spread _both computed without this patient's observation_.

This form of the PIT is the frequentist predictive distribution that includes **parameter uncertainty** — the exact analog of the Bayesian posterior-predictive PIT. In Stata it is obtained using: `predict t, rstudent` then `1 - ttail(e(df_r)-1, t)`.

<!--
Why not standardized residual?
Both put patient i's residual on a standard scale by dividing by an estimated standard deviation with the leverage correction $\sqrt{1-h_{ii}}$. The one difference that matters for the PIT is which σ estimate goes in the denominator, and whether that makes the ratio a statistic with a known distribution
Standardized: the same $e_i$ that sits in the numerator is also baked into $s$ in the denominator (every residual contributes to the full-sample RMSE). Numerator and denominator are correlated, so $r_i$ is not $t$-distributed — it's actually a rescaled Beta variable. Using a normal or $t$ CDF and the PIT is only approximately uniform.
Studentized (deleted): because $s_{(i)}$ is computed without patient i, the numerator $e_i$ and the denominator are independent. The ratio is exactly $t_{,n-p-1}$, so $u_i = T_{n-p-1}(t_i)$ is exactly Uniform(0,1).
 -->

```{stata}
*| eval: false
* Exact deleted-residual PIT, raw model
quietly regress los i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
scalar df_t = e(df_r) - 1
predict double rstud_raw, rstudent
generate double pit_raw_exact = 1 - ttail(df_t, rstud_raw)
histogram pit_raw_exact, width(0.05) percent fcolor(midblue%50) lcolor(white) ///
    yline(5, lpattern(dash) lcolor(red)) xtitle("exact PIT") ///
    title("Raw model: still not flat") name(pe_raw, replace)
* Exact deleted-residual PIT, log model
quietly regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
scalar df_t = e(df_r) - 1
predict double rstud_log, rstudent
generate double pit_log_exact = 1 - ttail(df_t, rstud_log)
histogram pit_log_exact, width(0.05) percent fcolor(midblue%50) lcolor(white) ///
    yline(5, lpattern(dash) lcolor(red)) xtitle("exact PIT") ///
    title("log model: flat") name(pe_log, replace)
graph combine pe_raw pe_log, rows(1)
qui graph export img/rhc_pit_exact.png, replace width(1600)
```

![Exact deleted-residual PIT for the raw-days and log models. The verdict is identical to the plug-in PIT: the raw model is not flat, the log model is.](img/rhc_pit_exact.png){width=85% .lightbox}

The exact PIT gives the **same verdict** and, with n ≈ 5700 and tiny leverage
($h_{ii}\approx p/n\approx 0.003$, so $t_{n-p-1}\approx$ normal), is numerically almost
indistinguishable from the plug-in here. The raw model stays non-uniform because the main problem
is the outcome **shape** not the plug-in approximation.

:::



## 6. Checking the assumptions, in severity order {#sec-assumptions}

::: panel-tabset

### Question

Now, after all that, the textbook checks. The chapter orders them by the **severity of
their consequences**:

1. correct **functional form** — biases coefficients;
2. **endogeneity** (predictors correlated with the error) — biases coefficients;
3. **independent errors** — affects standard errors;
4. **homoskedasticity** — affects standard errors;
5. **normal errors** — affects standard errors, least consequential.

Which of these actually matter for this LOS model?

::: {style="height: 400px;"}
:::

### Hint

Functional form: `acprplot`, `estat ovtest` (RESET), and AIC/BIC for the quadratic term.
Endogeneity: there is no command — argue it with a DAG. Independence: cluster the SEs.
Homoskedasticity: `rvfplot` and a robust-SE safety net. Normality: `qnorm`.

::: {style="height: 500px;"}
:::

### Answer-1

**1. Functional form.** Confirm the curvature modeled in `surv2md1`, and check the
quadratic (`p6a1_fnxn`):

```{stata}
quietly regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
capture noisily acprplot surv2md1, lowess lsopts(lcolor(cranberry)) ///
    title("Component-plus-residual: surv2md1 (linear fit)")
qui graph export img/rhc_ff_acpr.png, replace width(1400)
```

![Component-plus-residual plot for predicted survival under a linear specification, showing curvature the lowess fit tracks.](img/rhc_ff_acpr.png){width=70% .lightbox}


```{stata echo=2:6}
*| eval: true
quietly regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
estat ovtest
estimates store ff_linear
quietly regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
estimates store ff_quad
estimates stats ff_linear ff_quad
```

The Ramsey test suggests that there is an omitted variable or a non-linear relationship.

The AIC and BIC suggest that the model with the quadratic fits better than the one without.

### Answer-2

**2. Endogeneity.** There is rarely any way to check this from the data. OLS forces the fitted residuals to be mechanically uncorrelated with the predictors, so an omitted baseline confounder hides inside the (biased) coefficients, not in a residual plot. Satisfying the assumption can only be argued by design and theory — supported by a DAG drawn before fitting. 

There are some procedures for looking at how senstive your coefficients would be to an umeasured confounder (Oster/coefficient-stability sensitivity (`psacalc`)).  If you can think of a variable that effectively randomizes an exposure in the model then you can use this as an instrument and test using a Hausman test (`ivregress 2sls` then `estat endog`). 

As we pointed out in section 4: conditioning on in-hospital death by only analyzing survivors is endogenous **selection** — you cannot adjust your way out of endogeneity by adding a downstream variable.

::: {style="height: 300px;"}
:::

### Answer-3

**3. Independent errors.** 
(`p6a3_indep`)
Think about potential clustering of data.  For example, you could examine clustering within disease category (different diseases may have shared teams, protocols, pathways). Compare default and diagnosis-clustered SEs:

```{stata}
*| eval: true
quietly regress lnlos c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex i.cat1
estimates store se_default
quietly regress lnlos c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex i.cat1, vce(cluster cat1)
estimates store se_cluster
estimates table se_default se_cluster, keep(1.dnr1 age) b(%6.3f) se ///
title("Default vs. diagnosis-clustered standard errors")
```

### Answer-4

**4. Homoskedasticity.** 
(`p6a4_hetero`)

On the chosen log model the residual spread is roughly even
across fitted values (section 5 already showed the raw-days model fails badly); you can add 
robust-SE to be sure that the standard errors are not under-estimated if there is any residual heteroskedasticity:

```{stata}
quietly regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
rvfplot, yline(0) title("log LOS: residual spread roughly even")
qui graph export img/rhc_rvf_log.png, replace width(1400)
```

![Residuals-versus-fitted plot for the log model: spread is roughly even about zero.](img/rhc_rvf_log.png){width=70% .lightbox}

```{stata, echo=2:7}
*| eval: true
quietly regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
estimates store hs_default
quietly regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex, vce(robust)
estimates store hs_robust
estimates table hs_default hs_robust, keep(1.dnr1 age) b(%6.3f) se ///
    title("Default vs. heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors")
```

### Answer-5

**5. Normal errors** — the least consequential check (`p6a5_normal`):

```{stata}
quietly regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
predict r_log, resid
qnorm r_log, title("log LOS residuals: close to normal")
qui graph export img/rhc_qq_log.png, replace width(1400)
```

![Normal quantile plot of the log-model residuals: close to the reference line.](img/rhc_qq_log.png){width=70% .lightbox}

With n ≈ 5700 the CLT already protects the predictive comparisons, so normality was the
least consequential check. 

:::

## 7. Epilog: use Poisson instead of log-OLS {#sec-poisson}

::: panel-tabset

### Question

All the retransformation fuss in section 3 exists only because we logged the **outcome**.
Is there a model that gives **mean days directly**, with no smearing factor?

::: {style="height: 500px;"}
:::

### Hint

Poisson regression puts the log on the **link**, modeling `E(LOS|X) = exp(Xβ)` on the day
scale. With `vce(robust)` the Poisson pseudo-MLE is consistent for that mean even though
LOS is not a count and is over-dispersed (Gould 2011; Silva & Tenreyro 2006).

::: {style="height: 500px;"}
:::

### Answer

```{stata}
poisson los i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex, vce(robust)
margins cat1
marginsplot, horizontal recast(scatter) ///
    title("Poisson: predicted mean LOS by disease category") ///
    xtitle("Predicted LOS (days)")
qui graph export img/rhc_pois_cat.png, replace width(1400)
```

![Predicted mean LOS by disease category from the robust Poisson model, on the day scale with no retransformation.](img/rhc_pois_cat.png){width=70% .lightbox}

Side-by-side, the two methods for getting a mean on the day scale — log-OLS + Duan smearing, and
Poisson with robust SEs — reach a similar place:

```{stata}
*| eval: true
quietly regress lnlos i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex
capture drop er2 eer2
predict double er2, residuals
generate double eer2 = exp(er2)
summarize eer2, meanonly
scalar duan2 = r(mean)
quietly margins cat1, expression(duan2*exp(xb())) post
estimates store logols_duan
quietly poisson los i.cat1 c.surv2md1##c.surv2md1 i.dnr1 c.age i.sex, vce(robust)
quietly margins cat1, post
estimates store poisson_mean
estimates table logols_duan poisson_mean, b(%6.2f) se ///
    title("Predicted mean LOS by disease category: log-OLS+Duan vs Poisson")
```

The Poisson route needs no retransformation and carries its own robust standard errors —
so for a skewed, positive outcome like LOS, you can *use `poisson` rather than `regress`.*

:::

## Recap: 

In the end, we did not check the model to certify it afterword; we checked it as part of building it. In order of consequence:

- **Outcome scale** (sections 1, 2, 5): a naive normal-error model on raw days predicts
  impossible negative stays and is miscalibrated. Logging fixes both.
- **A hidden mixture** (sections 2, 4): the inverted-U in predicted survival is survivors
  and deaths running in opposite directions — you can describe them separately, but do not
  "adjust" for a downstream collider.
- **Confounding by design** (section 6, endogeneity): this problem can not be identifed in 
model checking it has to be argued
- **Standard-error assumptions** (section 6): independence, homoskedasticity, normality —
  the *least* consequential, and largely handled by the log scale, cluster or robust SEs, and a large enough sample.
